timeline.name: Pro Reverb
timeline.voice: Two twelves like a Twin Reverb, with two 6L6s instead of four.
timeline.story: Two twelves like a Twin Reverb, but two 6L6s instead of four, so it runs out of clean room sooner. Fender’s AA165 drawing follows the same plan as the Vibrolux Reverb: two channels with Volume, Treble, Bass and a Bright switch, then Reverb, Speed and Intensity on the Vibrato channel, with a tube-driven spring tank and optical tremolo. The difference is the power supply. The Pro Reverb has a bigger power transformer, about 440 volts on the plates, and stacked filter caps to handle it. It first shipped in mid-1965, after CBS bought Fender, so every one is a CBS amp, and some still say Fender Electric Instrument Co. on the panel.
timeline.ratingNote: Catalog row 71, 40 W. Circuit follows Fender drawing AA165 (D-FE), which shows a GZ34 rectifier; Premier Guitar says 5U4GB (Q31). Cabinet 19.5 × 26.5 × 9.5 in from Mojotone. Rear-panel wording from a September 1965 amp.

parts.label: High-voltage power supply
parts.title: More voltage than the Vibrolux on the same two tubes.
parts.body: The AA165 power transformer puts about 440 V on the plates of the two 6L6GCs, against about 410 V on the Vibrolux Reverb. The first filter is a 20 µF, 525 V cap, and the next stage uses two 70 µF, 350 V caps in series with 220K resistors across them to share the voltage.
attributes: 20 µF 525 V; 2 × 70 µF 350 V in series
parts.listen: More plate voltage means more clean room from the same two tubes.
parts.together: Series caps are how Fender got a high voltage rating out of lower-voltage parts. The 220K resistors keep the two caps splitting the voltage evenly.
parts.extra: Fender drawing AA165; drawing AA964 for the Vibrolux comparison.
parts.detail: Headroom is a reading of the drawing, not a measurement.
sources: Fender "Vibrolux Reverb-Amp AA964" schematic, drawing J-FD

parts.label: Rectifier tube
parts.title: A GZ34, according to Fender’s drawing.
parts.body: The AA165 drawing shows a GZ34 rectifier fed with 340 V AC on each side.
parts.listen: If you find a 5U4GB in one, that isn’t automatically wrong. It drops more voltage than a GZ34, so the amp would run a little cooler and softer.
parts.together: Guitarpoint’s tube chart for a 1965 amp also reads GZ34.
parts.detail: Premier Guitar says the stock rectifier is a 5U4GB. Not settled.

parts.label: Tube-driven spring reverb
parts.title: The reverb has its own tube and transformer.
parts.body: A 12AT7 drives the spring tank through a small transformer, and a 7025 recovers the return. The Reverb knob blends it back into the Vibrato channel.
parts.listen: The tank is driven hard, so a little Reverb goes a long way.
parts.together: The circuit matches the Vibrolux Reverb’s on Fender’s drawings.
parts.detail: The original tank isn’t in every surviving amp.

parts.label: Optical tremolo
parts.title: Tremolo on the Vibrato channel only.
parts.body: A 12AX7 oscillator flashes a lamp next to a light-dependent resistor, which pulses the Vibrato channel’s signal. Speed and Intensity are on that channel.
parts.listen: Plug into Normal and the tremolo isn’t there.
parts.together: Same plan as the Vibrolux Reverb.

parts.label: CBS-era back panel
parts.title: The back panel says CBS.
parts.body: The printed back panel reads Fender Musical Instruments, a division of Columbia Record Distribution Corp., and rates the speaker jack at 40 watts. It also has the ground switch, a 2 A slow-blow fuse, power and standby switches, an extension speaker jack, two pedal jacks and the reverb tank jacks.
parts.listen: The Pro Reverb arrived after the sale, so there’s no pre-CBS one to hunt for. Some still carry Fender Electric Instrument Co. on the front panel.
parts.together: Wikipedia dates the first Pro Reverbs to mid-1965.
parts.extra: A September 1965 amp’s back panel and Wikipedia.
parts.detail: Panel wording varied during the run.
sources: Mojotone field guide: Blackface Pro Reverb

parts.label: Two twelves at 4 ohms
parts.title: Two twelves in a cabinet a little smaller than a Twin.
parts.body: Two twelves at 4 ohms, Jensen C12N or Oxford 12L6 according to Mojotone, in a cabinet about 19.5 inches tall and 26.5 wide. Large chassis straps, tilt-back legs and chrome corners.
parts.listen: Twelves give it a bigger low end than the Vibrolux’s tens.
parts.together: The tilt-back legs are 16 inches long.
parts.detail: Dimensions are Mojotone’s; Fender’s figure wasn’t found.
sources: Mojotone field guide: Blackface Pro Reverb
